How the gridT method reconstructs temperature

A companion explainer for the TEXAS TEX86/Ring Index proxy — from one measured Ring Index to a full temperature posterior.

TEXAS turns a measured Ring Index (RI) into a sea-surface temperature by inverting a Bayesian calibration. The full inversion runs an MCMC (Stan) model; gridT is the fast stand-in that computes the same posterior by integrating it on a temperature grid. It reproduces the MCMC result to within 0.01 °C but runs in milliseconds.

The one idea We don't invert a single calibration curve. The forward calibration is an ensemble of ~100 RI–temperature curves that captures the calibration's own uncertainty. gridT asks, for every candidate temperature, how well does the whole ensemble reproduce the observed RI? — averages that, multiplies by an SST prior, and reads off a temperature distribution.
The estimator
p(T | RI)  ∝  p(T)  ×  (1/M) Σm 𝒩( RI | μm(T), σm )
μm(T) = bm + (1 − bm) / (1 + e−km(T − T0m))1/vm

Estimate = median of p(T|RI).   Uncertainty = its quantiles: 68% CI = [p16, p84], 90% CI = [p5, p95].
Averaging over the m draws before normalizing is the whole point — it folds calibration uncertainty into the answer.

The computation, unrolled

  1. Inputs. One Ring Index observation and the full ~100-curve calibration ensemble.
  2. Predict at a candidate T. Every curve predicts an RI; a good temperature is one whose predicted-RI cloud brackets the observation.
  3. Average the likelihood. Score the observed RI under each member's Gaussian and average across the ensemble → one number per temperature. (this is the (1/M)Σ in the code)
  4. Sweep T. Repeating over the grid traces the marginalized likelihood L(T).
  5. Apply the SST prior. Multiply L(T) by p(T).
  6. Read the posterior. Its median is the estimate (26.6 °C); its quantiles are the uncertainty (68% CI [23.1, 29.8]).

The reconstruction, start to finish

Where is the “grid”? (and how candidate T's are chosen)

The candidate temperatures aren't hand-picked — gridT lays down a regular ruler of temperatures and evaluates the posterior at every tick:

the grid
T = np.linspace(−1.8, 45, 4000)  # ~4000 temperatures, ~0.012°C apart

That comb of temperatures on the x-axis is the grid — it's why the method is called “grid”-T. It looked invisible in the earlier figures only because 4000 evaluations plotted as a line look continuous, and I marked just a few ticks as dots.

Only two choices define the grid: the range (must be wide enough to contain the posterior's mass — too short a top end clips warm/saturated tails, the one caveat noted below) and the resolution (more ticks = more accurate but slower; 4000 is far finer than the reported precision, so effectively exact). This is the one real difference from the Stan inverse, which draws MCMC samples from the same posterior instead of gridding it.

What the likelihood is (the fit-score)

Before averaging over the ensemble, gridT needs a score for a single curve: given a candidate temperature T, how well does it explain the RI you actually measured? That score is the likelihood L(T) = 𝒩(RI_obs | μ(T), σ).

How the miss becomes a number The proxy is noisy, so at a candidate T the observation scatters around the curve's prediction as a Gaussian of width σ. The likelihood is simply the height of that noise bell at your observed RI — tall at the fat centre (good fit), short in the thin tail (bad fit).

The formula L = exp[ −½ (miss/σ)² ] does three things to the miss: ÷σ (how many noise-widths off), square (positive, and big misses hurt disproportionately), exp(−½·) (map to a 0–1 score that decays like a Gaussian). Worked at σ = 0.058:

candidate Tprediction μ(T)missz = miss/σL = exp(−½ z²)
16 °C0.547+0.173+2.980.01
28 °C (best fit)0.7200.0000.001.00
34 °C0.827−0.107−1.850.18

This is one curve. The full method draws one such likelihood for each of the ~100 ensemble members and averages them (the marginalization, next), then multiplies by the prior.

Why marginalize? (vs. the naive single-curve inverse)

It matches the full Bayesian inversion

gridT integrates the exact density the MCMC model samples — same likelihood, same prior — so it is not an approximation with its own bias. Validated against a fine-grid reference on the real univ_priorApprox_SST_scaledRI_cren3 posterior:

quantilemax |Δ| (°C)RMS (°C)
p50 (median)0.0070.006
p16 / p840.0090.006
p5 / p950.0100.007
One caveat — saturated warm samples Near the top of the S-curve the proxy saturates and the posterior grows a long warm tail. Keep the temperature grid wide enough that this tail closes: a too-short grid truncates p95 by up to ~3 °C at RI ≈ 0.97. Flag any sample with non-negligible posterior mass at the grid edge.

30-second script (for the poster)

  1. "We measure Ring Index from the GDGTs."
  2. "Our calibration isn't one curve — it's an ensemble, so we carry its uncertainty."
  3. "For every temperature on a grid we score how well all the curves reproduce the observed RI, and average — that's the marginalization."
  4. "Times an independent SST prior gives a full temperature posterior. Median is the estimate, the spread is honest uncertainty."
  5. "It matches the full MCMC inversion to a hundredth of a degree, but fast."

Q&A

Isn't a grid just an approximation of the real Bayesian model?

It's numerical integration of the same posterior the MCMC samples — same likelihood, same prior. Validated to max |Δ| ≈ 0.01 °C for RI ≲ 0.80. No estimator difference, no Monte-Carlo noise.

Where does the temperature prior come from — doesn't it drive the answer?

Where RI is informative (the steep middle of the S-curve) the data dominate and the prior barely moves the median. The prior only matters at the saturated ends where the proxy carries little temperature information. We use a diffuse σ = 10 °C.

What happens for warm, saturated samples?

The proxy saturates near the top of the S-curve, so the posterior grows a long warm tail and the estimate becomes prior-dependent. We keep the grid wide enough that the upper tail closes and flag samples with mass at the grid edge.

Why not just report the plug-in point estimate?

It ignores calibration uncertainty and the prior, has no credible interval, and is undefined or explosive at the S-curve asymptotes (see the contrast figure).

How is the uncertainty defined — is it just calibration scatter?

It's the full posterior width: calibration-curve uncertainty (ensemble spread) + residual proxy scatter σm + prior, all propagated together. 68% and 90% credible intervals from the posterior CDF.

Does it use the GDGT-2/3 and NO₃ corrections?

The thermal (univariate) version shown here uses RI only. The multivariate model adds βG23·(GDGT-2/3) and βNO3·log(NO₃) (below a cutoff) to the curve's lower term; same marginalization, richer mean function.

How many calibration draws M, and does it matter?

~100 draws. The average is a Monte-Carlo estimate of the marginal likelihood; 100 is enough for the median and CI to stabilize at our reporting precision.

Could two temperatures give the same RI (non-identifiability)?

The curve is monotonic in T, so no — but sensitivity collapses at the flat ends, which is why those samples get wide intervals rather than a false-precise point.
